name: State of Katanga
recognition: Never gained general recognition; sources differ on Belgium
cost: 1,250 million Belgian francs advanced by Union Minière, about US$25 million
story: On 11 July 1960 Moïse Tshombe of the CONAKAT party declared the mining province of Katanga independent, with its capital at Élisabethville, now Lubumbashi. It covered 496,871 square kilometres and had about 1.7 million people. The mining company Union Minière du Haut-Katanga, which had held exclusive copper rights there since 1906, advanced Tshombe 1,250 million Belgian francs, about US$25 million. GlobalSecurity reports that the company had 1960 sales of over $200 million and that Katanga supplied 10% of the world's copper and 60% of its cobalt that year. In September 1960 about 1,133 Belgian technicians, 114 Belgian officers and 117 NCOs were attached to the government. In early 1961 nearly 500 British, Rhodesian, French and South African irregulars replaced expelled foreign fighters. Its currency was the Katangese franc. Wikipedia says Belgium gave de facto recognition on 16 July 1960, and GlobalSecurity says Belgium never officially recognised it while giving military, economic and technical help; the United States refused. UN forces launched Operation Grandslam on 28 December 1962 and held Élisabethville within three days. Tshombe conceded on 15 January 1963, and UN officials entered Kolwezi, his last stronghold, on 21 January.
mechanism: A mining region's revenue and a company's money can fund a breakaway government, and outside recognition and UN force decide whether it lasts.

name: Puntland
challenge: Withdrew recognition of the federal government on 31 March 2024
recognition: Federal member state of Somalia; it considers itself part of Somalia
story: Puntland is a semi-autonomous state in north-east Somalia, founded on 1 August 1998, with its capital at Garowe. It covers 212,510 square kilometres, and its 2016 population estimate was 4,334,633. It has its own constitution, inaugurated at a convention in April 2012, and it considers itself part of Somalia. On 31 March 2024 Puntland said it no longer recognised the authority of the federal government, would stop taking part in federal institutions, and would act independently until a constitution is approved in a referendum it takes part in.
mechanism: A region can run its own government and suspend ties with the centre while keeping the claim to be part of the state.

name: Territory of the Saar Basin
founder: Treaty of Versailles; League of Nations
story: The Treaty of Versailles took the Saar from German government for 15 years. Under Article 45 Germany ceded the coal mines to France as compensation for destroyed mines in northern France, and under Article 49 Germany renounced the government of the territory in favour of the League of Nations as trustee, with a vote on sovereignty after 15 years. A five-member Governing Commission ruled from 1920 and alone made law. A 30-member regional council, formed in 1922, could only advise. The territory had the Saar franc and its own postage stamps, and 812,000 people in 1933. On 13 January 1935, on a 98% turnout, 90.8% voted to rejoin Germany, 8.8% to keep the existing status and 0.4% to join France. The territory ended on 1 March 1935. After the Second World War it was a French-controlled protectorate from 1947 to 1956. A referendum on 23 October 1955 ended French rule, and the Saarland joined West Germany on 1 January 1957.
mechanism: A treaty can suspend a state's government over land for a fixed term and hand the final choice to the residents.

sources.t: Treaty of Versailles, Part III, Avalon Project

name: Memel Territory
founder: Treaty of Versailles; Principal Allied and Associated Powers
stopped_by: Lithuanian takeover in 1923, German ultimatum in 1939
laws: Treaty of Versailles, Article 99; Klaipėda Convention
recognition: Allied administration, then annexed by Lithuania, confirmed by convention
story: Under Article 99 of the Treaty of Versailles Germany renounced this 2,657 square kilometre territory on the Baltic in favour of the Allied powers. It was administered under the Conference of Ambassadors, first by the French general Dominique Odry from February 1920 and then by High Commissioner Gabriel Petisné from May 1921. In January 1923 the Klaipėda Revolt took place, and Lithuania occupied and annexed the territory. A convention of 8 May 1924 confirmed the annexation. A Lithuanian census in 1925 counted 141,000 people. After an oral German ultimatum, Lithuania's foreign minister Juozas Urbšys and Joachim von Ribbentrop signed a treaty ceding the territory to Germany on 23 March 1939.
mechanism: A territory left without a settled owner by treaty can be taken by a neighbour and later lost to a stronger one.

sources.t: Treaty of Versailles, Part III, Avalon Project

name: Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and Western Sirmium
founder: Croatian government and local Serb representatives, under the Erdut Agreement; UN Security Council
laws: Erdut Agreement; UN Security Council Resolution 1037
story: The Erdut Agreement of November 1995, between the Croatian government and local Serb representatives, set up a UN transition for this region along the Danube in eastern Croatia. Security Council Resolution 1037 established the UN Transitional Authority, UNTAES, on 15 January 1996. The Secretary-General first proposed 9,300 soldiers, and the final plan called for 5,000 soldiers, 500 civilian police and 99 military observers. At full deployment it had 4,849 soldiers, 99 observers and 401 police. Croatia refused to pay police salaries in Yugoslav dinars and the police refused kuna, so they were paid in Deutsche Marks. UNTAES helped hold the Croatian Chamber of Counties vote in the region on 13 April 1997. Its mission ended on 15 January 1998, and the UN says it peacefully reintegrated the territory into Croatia.
mechanism: A UN body can run disputed land for a fixed period with the aim of returning it to the state that claims it.

sources.t: United Nations Transitional Authority for Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and Western Sirmium

name: Telosa
recognition: None sought; a planned US city
cost: $400 billion proposed; over $25 billion for the first phase
story: In September 2021 the billionaire Marc Lore, a former Walmart executive, announced plans for Telosa, a new city on 150,000 acres of cheap land in the United States. The plan is for 5 million people over 40 years, at a stated cost of $400 billion, with a first phase of 50,000 people on 1,500 acres at over $25 billion, reported then for completion by 2030. Land would be licensed for building while residents share ownership through a community endowment, based on Georgist ideas. Fossil-fuel vehicles would be banned. No site had been chosen in the sources retrieved; Nevada, Utah, Arizona, Idaho, Texas and the Appalachian region were named as options. The map point marks Nevada as one of those options and is not a site.
mechanism: A private buyer can plan a city on bought land, and the land stays under state and national law.

sources.t: Former Walmart executive looking to build $400 billion smart city somewhere in US, KTNV

name: Fordlândia
stopped_by: Ford abandoned the town in 1934 and sold the land in 1945
laws: Brazilian law; export-tax exemption in exchange for 9% of profits
challenge: 1930 workers' revolt, ended by the Brazilian Army
recognition: None sought; a concession from Brazil
cost: Sold in 1945 at a loss of over US$20 million
story: In 1928 Henry Ford set up a company town on the Tapajós river in Pará, Brazil, to grow rubber for his cars, on a land concession of about 10,000 square kilometres. Ford was exempted from taxes on goods exported from Brazil in exchange for 9% of profits, 7% for the Brazilian government and 2% for local municipalities. Trees planted close together were easy prey for blight and insects. In 1930 workers revolted in the cafeteria over the food, cut telegraph wires and drove out managers until the Brazilian Army arrived and ended it. Ford Motor Company abandoned the town in 1934 and moved upriver to Belterra. In 1945 Henry Ford II sold the land to the Brazilian government at a loss of over $20 million. About 90 residents remained until the 2000s, and about 3,000 people lived there by 2017.
mechanism: A company can run a town on a state concession, and the state's army and law still apply there.

name: Goust
laws: French law; residents paid taxes in Laruns
story: Goust is a hamlet of 2.5 square kilometres on a plateau in the Pyrenees, part of the French commune of Laruns, reached by a mountain footpath across the Pont d'Enfer. Writers in the 19th century described it as an independent republic. The claim traces to an 1827 description by Joseph Lainé, and Samazeuilh wrote in 1858 that Lainé was speaking metaphorically and later writers took it literally. Residents paid taxes to the government in Laruns, and baptisms, weddings and burials took place at the church there. Late 19th-century US newspapers reported an uprising in 1896 over a newspaper ban, which remains unverified.
mechanism: A remote place can gain a reputation for independence through writers' accounts while its residents keep paying tax to the state.

name: Kīngitanga, the Māori King Movement
founder: Māori chiefs of the central North Island; first king Pōtatau Te Wherowhero
challenge: British invasion of Waikato, July 1863; 486,500 hectares confiscated
recognition: Monarchs not recognised by New Zealand law or by many iwi; the Waitangi Tribunal has addressed the 1840 cession
story: In the 1850s chiefs in the central North Island sought unity to slow European land purchases and a monarch whose status could match Queen Victoria's. Pōtatau Te Wherowhero was crowned at Ngāruawāhia in June 1858. In 1861 Tamihana wrote that Māori were a separate nation, and the colonial government saw the movement as a challenge to the British monarchy. Governor Grey issued an ultimatum on 9 July 1863, and troops crossed into Waikato three days later. The government confiscated 486,500 hectares from those it called rebels, including cultivated land and burial sites. After defeats including Ōrākau in 1864, King Tāwhiao and his followers withdrew into Ngāti Maniapoto territory, later called the King Country, and declared that Europeans crossing its boundary, the aukati, risked death. On 14 November 2014 the Waitangi Tribunal concluded that the rangatira who signed te Tiriti in February 1840 did not cede their sovereignty to Britain. It said this leaves open how and when the Crown acquired the sovereignty it exercises today.
mechanism: A people can form a rival authority to a colonial state, and force and confiscation can remove its land while the movement continues.

sources.t: Report on Stage 1 of the Te Paparahi o Te Raki Inquiry Released, Waitangi Tribunal

name: Sámi parliaments
founder: Sámi voters in Norway, Sweden and Finland
laws: Sweden's body must comply with Riksdag decisions
recognition: Representative bodies inside Norway, Sweden and Finland; Russia did not recognise the Kola assembly as of 2017
story: The Sámi have elected parliaments in three states. Norway's opened on 9 October 1989 in Karasjok, with 39 members from seven constituencies. Sweden's opened on 26 August 1993 in Kiruna, with 31 members, and its actions must comply with decisions of the Riksdag. Finland's opened on 2 March 1996 in Inari, with 21 members, and followed an elected Sámi delegation. All three elect every four years. In Russia the Kola Sámi Assembly was set up on 12 December 2010 in Murmansk, and as of 2017 federal and regional authorities did not recognise it as a legislative body. The parliaments share a Sámi Parliamentary Council, and a Conference of Sámi Parliamentarians has met every three years since 2005. The map point marks Karasjok.
mechanism: An Indigenous people can elect its own parliaments across several states while each body stays under the state where it sits.
